(b), in the case of fungible goods, be of fair average quality within the description. (c), be fit for the ordinary purposes for which such goods are used. That is the most important one. (d), run, within the variations the agreement permits, of even kind, quality, and quantity within each unit and among all units. (e), be adequately contained, packaged, and labeled as the agreement may require. And (f), conform to the promises or affirmations of fact made on the container or label.
Examples: detergent must clean, not damage the fabric or the washer, and match its label. A pencil must write and erase with ordinary effort.
It is strict liability. Usually there must be a defect at the time of sale, or a failure to give proper instructions. The seller's lack of knowledge is no defense. It is not negligence-based.

Who is a merchant? Section 2-104(1): one who deals in goods of the kind; or who by occupation holds itself out as having knowledge or skill about the practices or goods involved; or to whom such skill may be attributed because it employs an agent or broker who holds itself out that way. For § 2-314, the narrow, goods sense applies: you must be a merchant in goods of that kind. Isolated sellers are not merchants, though comment 3 says they must still disclose known hidden defects.
Used goods: the warranty applies, but only to the quality appropriate for used goods.

Privity, a preview. Section 2-318 has three alternatives; each state picks one. Alternative A: the buyer's family, household, and guests in the home, injured in person. Alternative B: any natural person who may reasonably be expected to use, consume, or be affected by the goods, injured in person. Alternative C: any person who may reasonably be expected to be affected, and injured, which is not limited to personal injury. And the seller cannot exclude § 2-318's coverage. We return to privity on Day 4.
Problem 3-9: does this seller make the merchantability warranty?
An accountant who makes stained-glass baubles and sells them at a semi-annual craft fair. Likely yes. She regularly makes and sells goods of that kind; the day job is not decisive.
A rental company that sells its oldest fleet cars every four months. Likely yes. Regular, recurring used-car sales.

A contractor whose work is 60 percent services and 40 percent materials, where clients pick the materials. A hybrid. The warranty rules still apply to the goods, and it is likely a merchant in what it regularly supplies.
A decorator paid a finder's fee by the client. No. The decorator is not the seller.
Problem 3-10: is there a breach?
A new mower fails on its fourth use. Likely yes. Early failure is circumstantial proof of a defect at the time of sale, unless there was misuse.

A bone in a salmon fillet. It depends on the approach. The problem cites Webster, no breach, against Mexicali Rose and Schafer. Outside the class materials, these are usually called the foreign-natural test, Webster, and the reasonable-expectation test, Schafer. A fillet sold as boneless is the stronger claim under the reasonable-expectation test.
Yarn whose color varies across five dye lots. Likely not a breach if within trade-usage variations, § 2-314(2)(d).

A car that meets all safety rules but rates low in crash tests. Likely not. Merchantability needs minimal safety, not top safety. It might be different under fitness if the buyer had stated a particular safety need.

Webster versus Blue Ship Tea Room, Massachusetts, 1964, is cited only. The casebook gives no facts. Outside the class materials: a diner ordered fish chowder at a Boston restaurant, a fish bone lodged in her throat, and a jury found for her on merchantability. The appeals court reversed. Bones are natural to New England fish chowder and to be expected, so the chowder was fit for its ordinary purpose.

segments.ask: A dentist sells her used office car to a neighbor. The transmission fails a week later. Did she make a warranty of merchantability?
segments.answer: No. She is not a merchant in cars. An isolated seller makes no merchantability warranty, though under comment 3 she must disclose known hidden defects.

segments.ask: A hardware store sells a ladder that collapses under normal use. The store had no idea of the defect. Is lack of knowledge a defense?
segments.answer: No. Merchantability is strict liability; the ladder was not fit for its ordinary purpose, § 2-314(2)(c).

segments.say: The trap. Merchantability needs a merchant with respect to goods of that kind. Fitness does not need a merchant at all.

Recap. Six standards, with fitness for ordinary purposes the most important. Strict liability. A merchant in goods of the kind. Used goods get a used-goods standard. Problem 3-9: regular sellers are merchants; finders are not sellers. Problem 3-10: early failure proves defect; the fish-bone split; trade variations; minimal safety.

segments.ask: Name the six merchantability standards.
segments.answer: Pass without objection in the trade; fair average quality if fungible; fit for ordinary purposes; even kind, quality, and quantity; adequately contained, packaged, and labeled; and conform to promises on the label.

segments.ask: What did the court hold in Webster, per the outside-the-materials note?
segments.answer: No breach. Bones are natural to New England fish chowder and to be expected.

segments.ask: Under § 2-318 Alternative A, who is protected?
segments.answer: The buyer's family, household, and guests in the home, who are injured in person.

episodes.title: Fitness for a particular purpose: § 2-315 and Ingram River

segments.say: Roadmap. Four elements, particular versus ordinary, the barge case, and how to disclaim.

Section 2-315. Four elements. One, the seller has reason to know the buyer's purpose. Two, the buyer has a particular purpose, not an ordinary one. Three, the seller has reason to know the buyer is relying on its skill or judgment to select or furnish suitable goods. Four, the buyer actually relies.
Two notes. The seller need not be a merchant. And the reliance need not be reasonable; it must be actual.
Particular versus ordinary, comment 2: shoes for walking are an ordinary purpose; shoes for mountain climbing are particular. But the use need not be unique, only different from the customary use.

Ingram River Equipment versus Pott Industries, Eighth Circuit, 1987, a note case. Ingram bought four tank barges with heating coils from the builder, Pott, to haul heavy petroleum products on the Mississippi and heat them so they would unload in cold weather. Pott argued: carrying and heating heavy oil is the ordinary use of coil-equipped barges. We have built more than 30 for exactly that. So no fitness warranty arose.

Held: a fitness warranty could arise. The buyer's use need not be unique. The question is whether it is sufficiently different from the customary use of the goods. That depends on whether the goods are tank barges, used for many cargoes, or heating-coil barges. It is like buying climbing shoes at a general shoe store versus a climbing store. A fact question, and the finding for Ingram stood.
Why it matters. It draws the line between § 2-315, particular purpose, and § 2-314, ordinary purpose.
When is there no reliance? When the buyer gives precise specifications, or insists on a particular brand.

Disclaiming fitness: it must be in writing and conspicuous. It need not mention fitness. For example: there are no warranties which extend beyond the description on the face hereof. And as is also works.

segments.ask: A buyer tells a paint store clerk: I need paint for a boat hull that sits in salt water. Pick one for me. The clerk picks a house paint, which peels off in a month. What warranty?
segments.answer: Fitness for a particular purpose. The seller had reason to know the particular purpose and the reliance, and the buyer actually relied.

segments.ask: Same, but the buyer says: give me five gallons of Brand X exterior, item number 1234.
segments.answer: No fitness warranty. A buyer who insists on a brand or gives precise specifications is not relying on the seller's judgment. Merchantability may still apply.

segments.say: The trap. Fitness disclaimers need a conspicuous writing but no magic word. Merchantability disclaimers need the word merchantability but may be oral.

Recap. Section 2-315: reason to know the particular purpose, reason to know of reliance, and actual reliance. Any seller. Ingram River: the use need only differ from the customary use. No reliance with specs or a brand. Disclaim in a conspicuous writing.

segments.ask: Must the seller be a merchant to give the fitness warranty?
segments.answer: No. Any seller can.

segments.ask: What did Ingram River say about whether the use must be unique?
segments.answer: It need not be unique, only sufficiently different from the customary use of the goods.

segments.ask: Give a sentence that disclaims fitness without using the word.
segments.answer: There are no warranties which extend beyond the description on the face hereof.

episodes.title: Title and the power to transfer: §§ 2-312 and 2-403, entrustment, and infringement

segments.say: Roadmap. The three-step title approach, voidable versus void title, entrustment, the definition of purchase, and infringement claims.

The approach. One, what rights did the seller purport to transfer? That is § 2-403. Two, did the buyer actually get good title? That is § 2-312. Three, if not, there is a breach. And most courts say a colorable third-party claim breaches the warranty even if the title later proves good. The buyer should not have to litigate to protect its title, comment 1.

Section 2-403(1). A purchaser gets the title its transferor had or had power to transfer. A buyer of a limited interest gets only that interest. A transferor with voidable title can pass good title to a good-faith purchaser for value. Voidable title arises from fraud, a dishonored check, deception about identity, a cash sale, or larcenous fraud. But a thief has void title, and passes nothing.

Entrustment, § 2-403(2) and (3). Entrusting goods to a merchant who deals in goods of that kind gives the merchant power to transfer all of the entruster's rights to a buyer in ordinary course. The classic: you leave your watch at a jeweler for repair, the jeweler sells it to a customer, and the customer keeps it.
Purchase is defined broadly, § 1-201(b)(29): sale, lease, pledge, security interest, gift, or any other voluntary transaction creating an interest in property.

Infringement claims under § 2-312(3): the claim must cast a substantial shadow on the buyer's use. The buyer need not prove the claim valid, only that it is substantial and reasonably likely to bring litigation.

segments.ask: A thief steals a bike and sells it to a good-faith buyer for value. The owner finds it. Who gets the bike?
segments.answer: The owner. A thief has void title and passes nothing, even to a good-faith purchaser. The buyer's remedy is against the thief for breach of the title warranty.

segments.ask: A fraudster buys a bike from the owner with a check that bounces, then sells it to a good-faith purchaser for value. Who gets it?
segments.answer: The good-faith purchaser. The fraudster had voidable title, which can pass good title to a good-faith purchaser for value under § 2-403(1).

segments.ask: An owner leaves a guitar at a music store that sells guitars, for repair. The store sells it to a customer in ordinary course. Who wins?
segments.answer: The customer. Entrustment to a merchant who deals in goods of the kind lets it transfer the entruster's rights to a buyer in ordinary course, § 2-403(2).

segments.say: The trap. Void versus voidable. Theft is void. Fraud, a bad check, or identity deception is voidable.

Recap. Section 2-403: you get what your transferor had, but voidable title can pass good title to a good-faith purchaser for value; void title passes nothing; entrustment to a merchant in goods of the kind empowers a sale to a buyer in ordinary course. Section 2-312: a colorable claim breaches; as is does not disclaim title; infringement claims must cast a substantial shadow.

segments.ask: Name three sources of voidable title.
segments.answer: Fraud, a dishonored check, deception about identity, a cash sale, or larcenous fraud.

segments.ask: Under most courts, does a colorable but ultimately invalid third-party claim breach the title warranty?
segments.answer: Yes. The buyer should not have to litigate to protect its title, comment 1.

segments.ask: Does purchase include a gift?

episodes.title: Output and requirements: § 2-306, Orange and Rockland, and Problems 4-1 and 4-2

segments.say: Roadmap. The quantity rule for output and requirements contracts, its two limits, the Hess oil case, and two problems.

Section 2-306(1). A term measuring quantity by the seller's output or the buyer's requirements means the actual output or requirements that occur in good faith. Except that no quantity unreasonably disproportionate to any stated estimate may be tendered or demanded. If there is no estimate, the benchmark is any normal or otherwise comparable prior output or requirements. Section 2-306(2): a lawful agreement for exclusive dealing imposes, unless otherwise agreed, a duty of best efforts on both sides, the seller to supply and the buyer to promote.

Strictly, § 2-306 is not a gap filler. It interprets a quantity term the parties chose. And it has two limits. One, good faith. Two, no quantity unreasonably disproportionate, judged by the parties' expectations and the degree of risk.

Comment 2's guidance. A shutdown for lack of orders can be in good faith. A shutdown merely to curtail losses is not. A sudden expansion of the plant is not covered. And a market price far above the contract price signals opportunism. For decreases, courts split: some apply only good faith, others apply both tests.

Orange and Rockland Utilities versus Amerada Hess, New York Appellate Division, 1977, a note case. A requirements contract for oil, with stated estimates based on the buyer's plans to burn the oil to make electricity for its customers. The buyer then doubled its requirements, seeking the extra oil in order to sell the additional quantity in the market. Outside the class materials, the contract price was fixed, oil's market price had risen far above it, and Hess refused to supply the excess.

Held: unreasonably disproportionate is a limit separate from good faith. It applies even where a party acts in complete good faith. It is judged by the parties' expectations, using five factors. One, the size of the excess over the estimate. Two, the seller's ability to foresee it. Three, the gap between the market and contract prices. Four, whether the market rise was fortuitous. Five, the reason for the increase. The doubling was unreasonably disproportionate.
Why it matters. A requirements buyer cannot use the contract to speculate on the market.

Problem 4-1. (a): a fixed quantity, 50,000 square feet a year. The buyer cannot cut to 20,000 without the seller's assent. Fixed quantity means the demand risk is the buyer's. (b): requirements, no estimate. The buyer's orders go 25,000, then 32,500, then 35,000, then jump to 60,000, its plant capacity, when the market rises to $1.15. The seller can resist that as disproportionate and opportunistic. (c): the buyer drops to 5,000 in a recession, when the market is 90 cents. The seller argues disproportion and that the buyer is buying elsewhere; but a genuine lack of orders may be good faith.

Problem 4-2, where prior requirements were 90,000 then 100,000, asks you to build two examples. Good faith but disproportionate: the buyer honestly lands a huge new customer and needs 400,000. Proportionate but bad faith: the buyer orders a normal 110,000 to resell at a higher market price, or orders only 85,000 because it is secretly buying cheaper elsewhere.

segments.ask: A requirements buyer with a stated estimate of 1,000 units honestly gains a giant new customer and demands 5,000 when the market price is double the contract price. Can the seller refuse the excess?
segments.answer: Likely yes. Even in complete good faith, a quantity unreasonably disproportionate to the stated estimate cannot be demanded, § 2-306(1) and Orange and Rockland.

segments.say: The trap. Two separate limits. A buyer can be in good faith and still demand a disproportionate quantity, or ask for a normal quantity in bad faith.

Recap. Section 2-306: actual output or requirements in good faith, and not unreasonably disproportionate to an estimate or normal prior quantities. Exclusive dealing implies best efforts. Orange and Rockland: disproportion is separate from good faith, with five factors.

segments.ask: List the Orange and Rockland factors.
segments.answer: Size of the excess over the estimate, the seller's ability to foresee it, the market-versus-contract price gap, whether the market rise was fortuitous, and the reason for the increase.

segments.ask: Under comment 2, is a shutdown merely to curtail losses in good faith?
segments.answer: No. A shutdown for lack of orders can be; one merely to curtail losses is not.

segments.ask: What does exclusive dealing imply under § 2-306(2)?
segments.answer: Best efforts by the seller to supply and the buyer to promote, unless otherwise agreed.

episodes.title: Open price: § 2-305, Mathis v. Exxon, and Problem 4-3

segments.say: Roadmap. Four subsections of § 2-305, the comment 3 safe harbor, the Exxon dealer case and the majority that rejects it, and three price puzzles.

Section 2-305(1). If the parties intend to contract without settling the price, the price is a reasonable price at the time for delivery in three cases. (a), nothing is said about price. (b), the price is left to be agreed and they fail to agree. (c), the price is to be fixed by an agreed market or other standard set by a third person, and it is not so set.

Subsection (2): a price to be fixed by the seller or the buyer means a price for him to fix in good faith. Subsection (3): if a price left to be fixed otherwise than by agreement fails to be fixed through one party's fault, the other may treat the contract as cancelled or fix a reasonable price himself. Subsection (4): if the parties intended not to be bound unless the price is fixed or agreed, and it is not, there is no contract. The buyer returns any goods, and the seller returns any payment.
Comment 3 gives a safe harbor: in the normal case, a posted price or a market price satisfies good faith.

Mathis versus Exxon, Fifth Circuit, 2002, a note case that has its own slides, so treat it like a main case. Exxon franchise dealers had to buy a minimum amount of gas each month at a price Exxon set, the dealer tank wagon price. The dealers claimed Exxon set that price to squeeze them out, so it could replace them with company-run stations.

Their evidence: Exxon planned to convert stations to company stores. The price exceeded the wholesale, or rack, price plus delivery. After 1994 Exxon barred dealers from buying cheaper gas from jobbers. And many dealers became unprofitable. Exxon's reply: its price was within the range competitors charged.

Held: the jury's bad-faith finding was upheld. Good faith under § 2-305(2) has a subjective and an objective part. Comment 3's posted-price safe harbor covers only the normal case, and an intent to drive the buyer out of business takes the case outside it, even when the price is in the competitive range.

The split. The majority rejects Mathis. Shell versus HRN, Texas 2004, and Autry versus BP, Eleventh Circuit 2009, hold that a commercially reasonable, non-discriminatory price is in good faith regardless of motive, for the sake of certainty.
Problem 4-3. A thousand sacks; on February 1 the market is $7.

(a). Price to be agreed at delivery. The seller demands $15. The market is $12. The buyer covers at $13. There is a contract, because the parties intended to be bound. The price is a reasonable price, about $12. The seller breached by demanding $15, and the buyer recovers its cover difference.

(b). The price is the Chicago Board price on March 15, but the board is closed that day. The March 13 price was $12. The buyer buys elsewhere at $11. The agreed standard failed, so the price is a reasonable price, about $12. The contract exists, and the buyer's rejection is likely a breach.

(c). The price is to be set by a third party both agree on, and the buyer refuses to name anyone. The market is $13. The failure is the buyer's fault, so under § 2-305(3) the seller may cancel, or fix a reasonable price, about $13, and sue.

segments.ask: A supplier with the right to set price charges a dealer exactly the posted market price, but internal emails show it wants to drive the dealer out. Under the majority view, is that good faith?
segments.answer: Yes, under Shell v. HRN and Autry v. BP: a commercially reasonable, non-discriminatory price is in good faith regardless of motive. Under Mathis, the motive could make it bad faith.

segments.say: The trap. Section 2-305(4): if the parties intended not to be bound without an agreed price, there is no contract at all. Look for that intent before applying the reasonable-price rule.

Recap. Section 2-305: a reasonable price at the time for delivery if nothing is said, they fail to agree, or the standard fails; a party-set price must be in good faith; a party at fault for the failure lets the other cancel or set a reasonable price; and intent not to be bound means no contract. Mathis: motive can defeat the safe harbor. The majority, HRN and Autry: it cannot.

segments.ask: What did the Mathis dealers claim Exxon was trying to do?
segments.answer: Squeeze them out with its set price so it could replace them with company-run stations.

segments.ask: Under § 2-305(3), what can the innocent party do if the other party's fault prevents fixing the price?
segments.answer: Treat the contract as cancelled or fix a reasonable price itself.

segments.ask: What is the comment 3 safe harbor?
segments.answer: In the normal case, a posted or market price satisfies good faith.

episodes.title: Delivery and payment: the core obligations, tender, and Problem 4-4

segments.say: Roadmap. Who owes what, the tender conditions, shipment under reservation, the seller's tender under § 2-503, the delivery gap fillers, the shipping terms, and the wheat problem.
Section 2-301: the seller must transfer and deliver conforming goods; the buyer must accept and pay.

Section 2-507(1): the seller's tender is a condition to the buyer's duty to accept and, unless otherwise agreed, to pay. Section 2-507(2): if payment is due on delivery, the buyer's right to keep the goods is conditional on paying.

Section 2-511: the buyer's tender of payment is a condition to the seller's duty to deliver. Any means current in the ordinary course of business works, unless the seller demands legal tender and gives the buyer reasonable time to get it. And payment by check is conditional: it is defeated if the check is dishonored.
So tenders are concurrent conditions unless otherwise agreed. The problems assume the seller tenders first.

Shipment under reservation, § 2-505(1): the seller gets the documents of title from the carrier and holds them until paid, in effect keeping a security interest. It does not take away the buyer's right to inspect before payment under § 2-310(b).

Seller's tender, § 2-503(1): the seller must put and hold conforming goods at the buyer's disposition and give any notice reasonably necessary for the buyer to take delivery. Tender must be at a reasonable hour, and the goods kept available for the period reasonably necessary for the buyer to take possession. And the buyer must furnish facilities reasonably suited to receiving the goods.

The defaults, unless otherwise agreed. Conforming means in accordance with the obligations under the contract, § 2-106(2). All goods in a single delivery, and payment due on that tender, § 2-307. Place: the seller's place of business, or residence; but if identified goods are known by both at contracting to be elsewhere, that place, § 2-308. Time: a reasonable time, § 2-309(1). Payment: due at the time and place the buyer receives the goods, and no credit is presumed, § 2-310(a). And cooperation: if one party fails to cooperate seasonably, the other is excused for resulting delay, and may proceed reasonably or treat the failure as a breach, § 2-311(3).

Shipping terms: F.O.B., free on board, and F.A.S., free alongside, § 2-319. C.I.F., cost, insurance, and freight, and C. and F., cost and freight, § 2-320. The slide says 2-329, but it is § 2-320. And ex-ship, § 2-322.
Problem 4-4. A hundred bushels at $4. The seller tenders first.

Only 95 bushels, plus a broken loading auger. Not a proper tender: the quantity is nonconforming, because all goods are due in a single lot. Whether the auger matters turns on who must load, a trade-usage question. The seller may cure.
Moldy wheat. Not a proper tender. Nonconforming goods.
Pick it up within 2 hours or I sell it. Probably not proper. The seller must hold the goods for the period reasonably necessary.
Pick up at a warehouse 300 miles away. Proper only if both parties knew at contracting that the identified goods were there, § 2-308(b).
The buyer brings a small truck and wants half now, half tomorrow. The seller's tender is fine. It is a single lot, and the buyer must furnish suitable facilities.
The seller arrives at the buyer's farm on time, but the buyer's bins aren't ready. The seller's tender is fine. The buyer failed to cooperate, and the seller is excused for the delay, § 2-311(3).

segments.ask: A contract says nothing about payment terms. The buyer receives the goods and says: I'll pay in 60 days. Is that allowed?
segments.answer: No. Under § 2-310(a), payment is due at the time and place the buyer receives the goods. No credit is presumed.

segments.say: The trap. Payment by check is conditional. If the check bounces, the seller's rights revive, which sets up reclamation under § 2-507 on Day 5.

Recap. The seller tenders conforming goods; the buyer accepts and pays; tenders are concurrent conditions. Tender under § 2-503: hold at the buyer's disposition, with notice, at a reasonable hour, for a reasonable period. Defaults: single lot, seller's place, reasonable time, payment on receipt, cooperation excuses delay.

segments.ask: What is the default place of delivery?
segments.answer: The seller's place of business, or residence; or the place identified goods were known by both at contracting to be, § 2-308.

segments.ask: Is a check an absolute payment?
segments.answer: No. It is conditional, defeated by dishonor, § 2-511.

segments.ask: What does shipment under reservation do?
segments.answer: The seller holds the documents of title until paid, in effect retaining a security interest, § 2-505(1). It doesn't remove the buyer's right to inspect before payment.

episodes.title: Inspection, acceptance, and rejection: the first pass, and Problem 4-5

segments.say: Roadmap. The right to inspect, payment before inspection, when acceptance happens, what follows from accepting versus rejecting, perfect tender, installment contracts, and cure. Day 4 goes deep on each; today is the map.

Section 2-513. Unless otherwise agreed, the buyer may inspect before payment or acceptance, at any reasonable place, time, and manner. For shipped goods, that can be after arrival. The buyer bears the cost of inspection, but recovers it if the goods are nonconforming and rejected. No inspection before payment under C.O.D., cash on delivery, or payment-against-documents terms.
Three distinctions. Accepting goods is not accepting an offer. Possession is not acceptance, because the buyer may be inspecting. And payment is not acceptance, § 2-512(2).

Section 2-512: if the buyer agreed to pay before inspection, a nonconformity does not excuse payment, unless it appears without inspection, or there is fraud that would justify enjoining a letter of credit.

Acceptance, § 2-606: the buyer accepts when, after a reasonable chance to inspect, it signifies acceptance, fails to make an effective rejection, or does any act inconsistent with the seller's ownership. Accepting part of a commercial unit accepts the whole unit.

Now the contrast. If the buyer accepts: it can't reject later, § 2-607(2). It must pay the contract price, § 2-607(1). The burden of proving nonconformity shifts to it, § 2-607(4). It must notify of breach within a reasonable time or be barred, § 2-607(3)(a). And it has only a small window to revoke, where the nonconformity substantially impairs value, § 2-608.

If the buyer rejects: it must reject within a reasonable time with seasonable notice, § 2-602(1). It may not exercise ownership, § 2-602(2)(a). If in possession, it must hold with reasonable care for the seller, § 2-602(2)(b). A merchant buyer must follow the seller's reasonable instructions and sell perishables, § 2-603, and may store, reship, or resell, § 2-604. And it must state curable defects or lose them, § 2-605.

Effective versus rightful. Rejecting conforming goods can be effective but wrongful; that is the buyer's breach, § 2-703. Rejecting nonconforming goods is rightful; the buyer has remedies, §§ 2-601 and 2-711.

Perfect tender, § 2-601: if the goods or the tender fail in any respect to conform, the buyer may reject all, accept all, or accept any commercial units and reject the rest. Installment contracts, § 2-612: the buyer may reject an installment only if the nonconformity substantially impairs that installment and can't be cured; and there is a breach of the whole only if the whole contract's value is substantially impaired. Cure, § 2-508: the seller may cure within the contract time on seasonable notice, or get a further reasonable time if it reasonably thought the tender would be acceptable.

Problem 4-5. (a): the seller demands payment before inspection. The buyer is right to refuse; it may inspect first unless otherwise agreed. (b): the buyer wants a two-week lab test for genetically modified organisms, GMO. That is reasonable only if GMO-free is a contract term and the test is a reasonable manner and time. The buyer may hold the wheat for testing without accepting. The buyer pays the test costs unless the wheat fails and is rejected. Best practice: agree on a protocol in advance.

segments.ask: Buyer pays for goods on arrival, then inspects the next morning and finds defects. Seller says: you paid, so you accepted. Who is right?
segments.answer: Buyer. Payment is not acceptance, § 2-512(2), and the buyer had a right to a reasonable inspection first.

segments.say: The trap. Effective and rightful are different questions. A buyer can effectively reject conforming goods, and then it is the one in breach.

Recap. Inspect before paying unless otherwise agreed or C.O.D. Possession and payment are not acceptance. Acceptance under § 2-606 by signifying, failing to reject, or acting inconsistently with the seller's ownership. Accepting triggers price, notice, burden, and only revocation. Rejecting triggers timely notice, care, and particularizing defects.

segments.ask: What are the three ways a buyer accepts under § 2-606?
segments.answer: Signifying acceptance after a reasonable chance to inspect, failing to make an effective rejection, or doing an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership.

segments.ask: After acceptance, who bears the burden of proving a breach?
segments.answer: The buyer, § 2-607(4).

segments.ask: Under § 2-513, who pays for inspection?
segments.answer: The buyer, but it recovers the cost if the goods are nonconforming and rejected.

episodes.title: Risk of loss: the principles, the decision tree, and Problem 4-6

segments.say: Roadmap. What risk of loss is, the three principles, what happens when goods are destroyed, the seven-step decision tree, and the merchant split in Problem 4-6.
Risk of loss is about who bears a casualty to the goods: fire, theft, flood. It is not the same as performance or breach. And it is not tied to title.
Three principles. Risk goes to the party who controls the goods, best able to avoid loss. To the party most likely insured, comment 3 to § 2-509. And to the party in breach, § 2-510.

What happens when goods are destroyed? If the seller bears the risk: for unique or identified goods, the seller may be excused, § 2-613; for fungible goods, the seller must still tender. If the buyer bears the risk: the buyer must pay, § 2-709(1)(a).

The sequence. One, what is the seller's tender obligation, under §§ 2-307 to 2-309, 2-503, and 2-504? Two, has anyone breached, sending you to § 2-510 rather than § 2-509? Three, apply the right rule: carrier, bailee, seller's tender with the merchant split, or other agreement.
Now the decision tree. Seven steps. Say them with me.
One. Agreement on risk? Follow it, § 2-509(4). And in a sale on approval, risk stays with the seller until acceptance, § 2-327.

Two. Seller in breach? A nonconforming tender leaves risk with the seller until cure or acceptance, § 2-510(1). And on a rightful revocation, the buyer may treat the risk as the seller's from the beginning, to the extent of the buyer's insurance gap, § 2-510(2).

Three. Buyer in breach, for example by repudiating, as to identified conforming goods? Risk is on the buyer for a commercially reasonable time, to the extent of the seller's insurance gap, § 2-510(3).
Four. Carrier, shipment contract, which is presumed. Risk passes on due delivery to the carrier, § 2-509(1)(a).
Five. Carrier, destination contract. Risk passes when the goods are duly tendered at the destination, § 2-509(1)(b).

Six. Bailee, goods not moved. Risk passes on the buyer's receipt of a negotiable document of title, on the bailee's acknowledgment of the buyer's right, or a reasonable time after a non-negotiable document or delivery order, § 2-509(2).

Seven. Everything else, where the seller delivers or the buyer picks up. A merchant seller: risk passes on the buyer's receipt, physical possession. A non-merchant seller: risk passes on tender, § 2-509(3).
Why the merchant split? Comment 3. A merchant seller still controls the goods and can insure them, so risk stays with it, even if the buyer has paid.
Problem 4-6, non-shipment contracts.

(a). The seller drives the wheat in its own truck, and the truck burns on the way. The seller's own truck is not a carrier, so § 2-509(3) applies. Merchant seller: no receipt, so seller's risk. Non-merchant seller: risk passes on completion of tender, which never happened, so seller's risk. Seller bears it either way. And because the wheat is fungible, the seller must re-tender.

(b). The seller says: ready for pickup. A fire destroys the wheat before the buyer arrives. Merchant seller: the seller bears the loss, because there was no receipt. Non-merchant: the buyer bears it, because tender was complete. Merchant status decides the case.

segments.ask: A furniture store tells a customer, your paid-for sofa is ready for pickup. That night the store burns. Who bears the loss?
segments.answer: The store. A merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer's receipt, § 2-509(3), even though the buyer paid.

segments.ask: A neighbor sells his used sofa, tells the buyer it's ready, and leaves it in the open garage. That night it is stolen. Who bears the loss?
segments.answer: The buyer, if the neighbor duly tendered. A non-merchant seller passes the risk on tender, § 2-509(3).

segments.say: The trap. The seller's own truck is not a carrier. Title has nothing to do with risk.

Recap. Risk follows control, insurance, and breach. The tree: agreement, seller's breach, buyer's breach, shipment contract, destination contract, bailee, and everything else with the merchant split: merchant on receipt, non-merchant on tender.

segments.ask: Run the seven-step risk-of-loss tree.
segments.answer: Agreement; seller in breach, § 2-510(1) and (2); buyer in breach, § 2-510(3); shipment contract, on delivery to the carrier; destination contract, on tender at the destination; bailee, § 2-509(2); otherwise merchant on receipt, non-merchant on tender.

segments.ask: In a sale on approval, when does risk pass?
segments.answer: On acceptance, § 2-327.

segments.ask: Why does a merchant seller keep risk until receipt?
segments.answer: It still controls the goods and is likely insured, comment 3.

episodes.title: Shipment versus destination, § 2-504, Problem 4-7, Windows v. Jordan Panel, and bailees

segments.say: Roadmap. The two kinds of carrier contracts, the presumption, the seller's shipping duties, the trade terms, the custom-windows problem, and goods held by a warehouse.

A shipment contract, the norm: risk passes when the goods are duly delivered to the carrier. The buyer bears transit loss, and sues the carrier or claims on its insurance. Signals: F.O.B. seller's city; ship to; C.I.F. or C. and F. Title passes at shipment, § 2-401(2)(a).

A destination contract: risk passes when the goods are duly tendered at the destination. The seller bears transit loss. Signals: F.O.B. buyer's city; the seller expressly agrees to deliver at a place; ex-ship. Title passes on tender at the destination.
The presumption: a shipment contract, unless the seller expressly took responsibility during transit. Naming a destination, or paying the freight, does not make it a destination contract.

The seller's duties in a shipment contract, § 2-504. (a), put the goods in the carrier's possession and make a reasonable contract for their transportation. (b), obtain and promptly deliver any documents needed. (c), promptly notify the buyer of the shipment. And the limit: failure on (a) or (c) is a ground for rejection only if material delay or loss results.

The terms. C.I.F. means the price includes cost, insurance, and freight. The seller ships, insures, and tenders the documents; the buyer pays against documents, with no inspection first. It is still a shipment contract. C. and F. is the same minus insurance. F.A.S. means deliver alongside the vessel.
A buyer bearing transit risk is not helpless. It can sue the carrier, § 2-722 and Article 7, or claim on its insurance. And the seller keeps an insurable interest while it has title, § 2-501.
Problem 4-7. Custom windows shipped from South Dakota to New York.
(a). The contract says delivered to the site. The windows are properly packaged and destroyed in transit. The buyer bears the loss. It is a shipment contract, as in Windows versus Jordan Panel.
(b). The contract says delivered at the site. Arguably the seller bears it, as a destination contract.
(c). How do you make it a destination contract? Say F.O.B. buyer's site, or: the seller bears the risk until tender at the site.
(d)(1). The windows were improperly packaged, and the packaging caused the damage. The seller bears it. An improper shipment caused the loss, §§ 2-504 and 2-510(1).

(d)(2). The damage was caused by the carrier's fault, and on the slide, the windows were properly packaged. The buyer bears it. Risk already passed; sue the carrier. And even with bad packaging, there is no shift unless the packaging caused the loss.

Windows, Incorporated versus Jordan Panel Systems, Second Circuit, 1999, is cited only, behind this problem. The casebook gives the facts: a South Dakota seller of custom windows, a contract to ship them properly crated and delivered to the buyer's New York construction site, and damage in transit. Outside the class materials, the carrier's truck had an accident, the buyer refused to pay, and the seller sued for the price. The court held for the seller. Delivered to did not create a destination contract, so risk passed on delivery to the carrier. And even if the packing was inadequate, the accident, not the packing, caused the loss.

Goods held by a bailee, like a warehouse, and not moved. Tender under § 2-503(4): give the buyer a negotiable document of title, or get the bailee's acknowledgment of the buyer's right. A non-negotiable document or delivery order works unless the buyer seasonably objects, and the risk stays on the seller until the buyer has a reasonable time to present it.
Insurable interest, § 2-501: the buyer gets one on identification of the goods. The seller keeps one while it has title or a security interest.

segments.ask: A seller in Ohio ships goods to a buyer in Texas. The contract says: ship to buyer's Dallas warehouse; seller pays freight. The goods are lost in transit through no one's fault. Who bears the loss?
segments.answer: The buyer. It is presumed a shipment contract; naming a destination or paying freight doesn't change that. Risk passed on due delivery to the carrier, § 2-509(1)(a).

segments.ask: Same, but the seller never notified the buyer of the shipment, and the loss had nothing to do with that.
segments.answer: Still the buyer. Failure to notify under § 2-504(c) justifies rejection only if material delay or loss results, and the loss wasn't caused by it.

segments.say: The trap. Shipment is presumed. Ship to, delivered to, and paying freight are all still shipment contracts. You need F.O.B. destination or an express assumption of transit risk.

Recap. Shipment contracts pass risk on delivery to the carrier; destination contracts on tender at the destination; shipment is presumed. Section 2-504: proper carriage contract, documents, notice; failures on (a) or (c) count only if material delay or loss results. Windows v. Jordan Panel: delivered to was a shipment contract, and the accident, not the packing, caused the loss.

segments.ask: Name the three § 2-504 duties of a seller in a shipment contract.
segments.answer: Put the goods in the carrier's possession under a reasonable transport contract, obtain and deliver needed documents, and promptly notify the buyer.

segments.ask: Is a C.I.F. contract a shipment or destination contract?
segments.answer: A shipment contract.

segments.ask: When does a buyer get an insurable interest?
segments.answer: On identification of the goods, § 2-501.

episodes.title: Day 2 closing quiz

segments.say: Cumulative quiz, Days 1 and 2. Answer out loud.

segments.ask: A seller says: this is the finest wine in the region. Warranty or puffing?
segments.answer: Puffing. It is commendation, general and immeasurable.

segments.ask: In Rogath, if the buyer learned of the doubts only from a Tate curator, is he barred?
segments.answer: No. Knowledge from a third party doesn't bar recovery; he may have bought the warranty as insurance.

segments.ask: What is the most important merchantability standard?
segments.answer: Fit for the ordinary purposes for which such goods are used, § 2-314(2)(c).

segments.ask: A buyer gives the seller precise specifications. Is there a fitness warranty?
segments.answer: Generally no, because the buyer isn't relying on the seller's skill.

segments.ask: Can as is disclaim the warranty of title?
segments.answer: No. Title needs specific language or circumstances, § 2-312(2).

segments.ask: An owner's car is stolen and sold to a good-faith buyer. Who wins?
segments.answer: The owner. A thief has void title.

segments.ask: What did the court hold in Orange and Rockland?
segments.answer: That unreasonably disproportionate is a limit separate from good faith, and doubling the requirements to resell oil was unreasonably disproportionate.

segments.ask: What is the majority rule against Mathis?
segments.answer: A commercially reasonable, non-discriminatory price is in good faith regardless of motive, Shell v. HRN and Autry v. BP.

segments.ask: The contract is silent on delivery time. When must the seller deliver?
segments.answer: Within a reasonable time, § 2-309(1).

segments.ask: A merchant seller in a shipment contract delivers goods to the carrier; they are lost in transit. Who bears the loss?
segments.answer: The buyer. In a shipment contract risk passes on delivery to the carrier, regardless of merchant status.

segments.ask: A seller tenders nonconforming goods; while the buyer is deciding, a fire destroys them. Who bears the loss?
segments.answer: The seller. A nonconforming tender leaves risk on the seller until cure or acceptance, § 2-510(1).

segments.ask: From Day 1: what two things must a firm offer be in, and by whom?
segments.answer: In a signed record, by a merchant.

segments.ask: From Day 1: in Daitom, what was the knock-out rule's source?
segments.answer: Comment 6 to § 2-207.

segments.say: That's Day 2. Tomorrow: disclaimers, remedy limits, parol evidence, assignment, termination, repudiation, and excuse.

days.title: Disclaimers, remedy limits, parol evidence, assignment, termination, repudiation, and excuse

episodes.title: Spaced review of Days 1 and 2

segments.say: Welcome to Day 3. Five minutes of review first. Answer out loud.

segments.ask: What makes the Code's battle-of-the-forms rule different from the common law's?
segments.answer: Section 2-207 abolishes the mirror-image and last-shot rules. An expression of acceptance with different terms still forms a contract unless expressly conditional.

segments.ask: Name the four § 2-201 exceptions with their sections.
segments.answer: Merchant's confirmation, (2); specially manufactured goods, (3)(a); admission, (3)(b); part performance, (3)(c).

segments.ask: What are the two halves of good faith?
segments.answer: Honesty in fact and observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing.

segments.ask: In Roth Steel, what did Sharon threaten?
segments.answer: To stop selling Roth any steel in the second half of 1973 unless Roth paid more.

segments.ask: Name the three ways to create an express warranty.
segments.answer: An affirmation of fact or promise, a description, and a sample or model, each part of the basis of the bargain.

segments.ask: Under Rogath, when does a buyer's knowledge waive a warranty?
segments.answer: When the seller disclosed the facts making it false and the buyer closes without expressly preserving its rights.

segments.ask: What four elements make a fitness warranty?
segments.answer: Seller has reason to know the particular purpose, the purpose is particular, seller has reason to know of reliance, and the buyer actually relies.

segments.ask: What is entrustment?
segments.answer: Entrusting goods to a merchant who deals in goods of that kind gives it power to transfer all the entruster's rights to a buyer in ordinary course, § 2-403(2).

segments.ask: What are the two limits in § 2-306?
segments.answer: Good faith, and no quantity unreasonably disproportionate to a stated estimate or normal prior quantities.

segments.ask: A merchant seller tells the buyer the goods are ready. They burn before pickup. Who bears the loss?
segments.answer: The seller. A merchant's risk passes only on the buyer's receipt.

segments.ask: What is the presumption about carrier contracts?
segments.answer: A shipment contract, unless the seller expressly took responsibility in transit.

segments.say: Now, disclaimers.

episodes.title: Varying the Code: § 1-302 and Problem 5-1

segments.say: Roadmap. Freedom of contract under the Code, its limits, and the provisions you cannot vary.

Section 1-302. The parties may vary the effect of UCC provisions by agreement, with exceptions. One, the obligations of good faith, diligence, reasonableness, and care cannot be disclaimed. But the parties may determine the standards for measuring them, if not manifestly unreasonable. And where the Code requires action within a reasonable time, the parties may fix a specific time, if not manifestly unreasonable. Two, some provisions cannot be varied at all.

Which ones? Problem 5-1(b) lists them: § 2-302, unconscionability. Section 2-102, scope. Sections 2-204 to 2-207, formation. Section 2-403, the rights of third-party purchasers. And comment 1 adds § 2-201, the statute of frauds.

Problem 5-1(a) is a drafting exercise. A buyer wants a good-faith standard for a fuel price the seller sets. Tie the price to an objective index, or to the seller's lowest price to similar customers. Or simply use an index price instead. The seller, for its part, wants to limit the buyer's requirements. Use a stated estimate with a minimum and maximum, define requirements as fuel actually consumed by the existing fleet, and require notice of changes.

segments.ask: A contract says the buyer must reject within one hour of delivery of a complex machine. Is that enforceable?
segments.answer: Probably not. Parties may fix a reasonable time, but not one that is manifestly unreasonable, § 1-302(b). One hour for a complex machine likely is.

segments.say: Recap. You can vary most of the Code. You cannot disclaim good faith, diligence, reasonableness, or care, but you can set standards that are not manifestly unreasonable. And you cannot vary unconscionability, scope, formation, third-party purchasers' rights, or the statute of frauds.

segments.ask: Name the provisions Problem 5-1(b) says cannot be varied.
segments.answer: Section 2-302, § 2-102, §§ 2-204 to 2-207, and § 2-403, plus § 2-201 under comment 1.

segments.ask: Can parties set the standard for good faith?
segments.answer: Yes, if the standard is not manifestly unreasonable.

segments.ask: How would a buyer police a seller-set fuel price?
segments.answer: Tie it to an objective index or to the seller's lowest price to similar customers.

episodes.title: Warranty disclaimers: § 2-316 and Problems 5-3, 5-4, and 5-5

segments.say: Roadmap. How to disclaim each warranty, what conspicuous means, two threshold questions, the continuum of protection, and three problems.
Take each warranty in turn.

Express warranties. Nearly impossible to disclaim if they are part of the basis of the bargain. Under § 2-316(1), words creating a warranty and words negating it are read consistently where reasonable; where they can't be reconciled, the negation is inoperative. The seller's real defense is the parol evidence rule, which we reach later today.
Merchantability, § 2-316(2). No writing needed; oral is fine. If written, it must be conspicuous. And it must mention merchantability.
Fitness, § 2-316(2). It must be in writing and conspicuous. But it need not mention fitness. There are no warranties which extend beyond the description on the face hereof is enough.

All implied warranties, § 2-316(3). Three routes. (a), expressions like as is or with all faults. (b), examination. If the buyer examined the goods, or refused to examine after the seller demanded, there is no implied warranty as to defects an examination ought to have revealed. Only those defects. (c), course of dealing, course of performance, or usage of trade.

Title. Section 2-316 doesn't apply. Title is disclaimed only by specific language or by circumstances, like a sheriff's sale or an executor's sale, under § 2-312(2). As is fails. No writing, no conspicuousness requirement, but specific language.

Conspicuous, § 1-201(b)(10): so written that a reasonable person against whom it operates ought to have noticed it. Capitals, larger type, contrasting type or color. And it is a question for the court.

Before you apply § 2-316, ask two threshold questions. One, did the implied warranty arise at all? Two, is the disclaimer part of the contract? A disclaimer in a later form is a material alteration under § 2-207, so it is usually not part of the deal.

The continuum of protection. At the freedom-of-contract end: specially made commercial goods. Then merchant-to-merchant commercial goods. Then used goods. And at the paternalism end: prepackaged new consumer goods.

Problem 5-3 asks for every way to disclaim fitness. A conspicuous writing, which need not say fitness. No warranties beyond the face hereof. As is or with all faults. The buyer's examination, or refusal after the seller's demand. And course of dealing, course of performance, or usage of trade.

Problem 5-4. A fisherman buys an engine for his boat. The disclaimer is on the back of a delivery receipt. Both implied warranties arose: the dealer is a merchant, and the buyer gave the boat's specs and relied on the dealer's recommendation, which is fitness. A post-sale receipt term is likely not part of the contract, under §§ 2-207 and 2-209. If it is, it mentions merchantability and covers all implied warranties, but is it conspicuous on the back of a receipt? If the buyer is a consumer, additional terms are mere proposals, and consumer law may void the disclaimer. And if the dealer were not a merchant, there would be no merchantability warranty at all, though fitness could still arise.

Problem 5-5, title. When does a buyer accept an express title disclaimer? When provenance is uncertain and the price reflects the risk, like a quitclaim-style deal at an estate or liquidation sale. And circumstances alone can disclaim: storage-unit auctions, executor, trustee, or police auctions, and lien sales.

segments.ask: A merchant's signed contract says in bold capitals: SELLER DISCLAIMS ALL IMPLIED WARRANTIES OF FITNESS. Does it disclaim merchantability?
segments.answer: No. A merchantability disclaimer must mention merchantability, § 2-316(2). This one only reaches fitness.

segments.ask: A car dealer says orally at the lot: no warranty of merchantability on this one. The buyer signs a contract that says nothing about warranties. Is merchantability disclaimed?
segments.answer: It can be. A merchantability disclaimer may be oral if it mentions merchantability, but watch the parol evidence rule if the writing is final.

segments.ask: A buyer inspects a used tractor and misses a cracked block a reasonable inspection would have found. Is there an implied warranty as to the crack?
segments.answer: No, under § 2-316(3)(b). Examination removes implied warranties as to defects an examination ought to have revealed.

segments.say: The traps. Merchantability: the magic word, writing optional. Fitness: a conspicuous writing, no magic word. As is works for both implied warranties but not for title. And always check that the disclaimer is part of the contract.

Recap. Express warranties are nearly impossible to disclaim; the seller's defense is the parol evidence rule. Merchantability: mention it, conspicuous if written. Fitness: conspicuous writing. All implied: as is, examination, or trade practice. Title: specific language or circumstances.

segments.ask: What does conspicuous mean?
segments.answer: Written so a reasonable person against whom it operates ought to have noticed it, decided by the court.

segments.ask: What are the two threshold questions before § 2-316?
segments.answer: Did the implied warranty arise, and is the disclaimer part of the contract?

segments.ask: Name two circumstances that disclaim title without words.
segments.answer: A sheriff's or executor's sale, storage-unit auctions, police auctions, lien sales.

episodes.title: Remedies: the framework and the damage types

segments.say: Roadmap. The four elements of a claim, disclaimers versus remedy limits, the damage types, and the table of breaches and remedies. Days 4 and 5 go deep; this is the map.

The framework: contract, breach, damages, causation. A disclaimer removes the breach, because there is no warranty to breach. A remedy limitation limits damages after a breach: liquidated damages, a limited remedy, or a consequential-damages exclusion. And always ask two things: what happened to the goods, and how are damages calculated?

The damage types. Compensatory. Incidental, § 2-715(1): the reasonable costs of responding to the breach, like inspection, transport, storage, and arranging cover. Consequential, § 2-715(2): losses from the buyer's requirements and needs that the seller had reason to know at contracting and that the buyer couldn't reasonably prevent, plus injury to person or property from a breach of warranty. Examples: lost profits from a production shutdown, or a fire caused by a defective oven. And liquidated, § 2-718.
The table. Say it as five breaches.

The seller repudiates or doesn't deliver. The buyer cancels, recovers the price paid, and gets market minus contract, § 2-713, or cover minus contract, § 2-712, plus incidental and consequential. Specific performance only rarely, § 2-716.

The seller tenders nonconforming goods. The buyer rejects, and it is the same as nondelivery. Or the buyer accepts, pays the price, and recovers value as warranted minus value as accepted, § 2-714(2), plus incidental and consequential.
The buyer revokes acceptance. Cancel, recover the price, take cover or market damages, plus incidental and consequential.

The buyer repudiates or wrongfully rejects. The seller withholds or stops delivery, cancels, and recovers resale minus contract, § 2-706, or contract minus market, § 2-708(1), or lost profit, § 2-708(2), plus incidental. A prepaying buyer gets restitution less the seller's damages, § 2-718(2).
The buyer accepts but doesn't pay. The seller recovers the price, § 2-709, plus incidental. And rarely, it may reclaim the goods, §§ 2-507(2) and 2-702(2).
Remedy limitations: ask two questions. One, is it part of the agreement? Two, is it enforceable? And limitations are never implied.

segments.ask: A buyer's claim for lost profits from a factory shutdown: incidental or consequential?
segments.answer: Consequential, § 2-715(2).

segments.say: Recap. A disclaimer kills the breach; a limitation shrinks the damages. Incidental damages are costs of responding to the breach. Consequential damages are foreseeable losses the buyer couldn't prevent, plus injury to person or property. The buyer's remedies turn on whether it rejected, accepted, or revoked; the seller's on who has the goods.

segments.ask: What is the buyer's measure if it accepts nonconforming goods?
segments.answer: Value as warranted minus value as accepted, § 2-714(2), plus incidental and consequential.

segments.ask: What are the seller's three damage measures when the buyer repudiates?
segments.answer: Resale, § 2-706; market, § 2-708(1); and lost profit, § 2-708(2); each plus incidental.

segments.ask: What two questions do you ask about a remedy limitation?
segments.answer: Is it part of the agreement, and is it enforceable?

episodes.title: Liquidated damages: § 2-718(1), Problem 5-6, and Problem 5-9

segments.say: Roadmap. The three-part reasonableness test, penalties, down payments, the oven problem, and how liquidated damages differ from remedy limitations.

Section 2-718(1). Damages may be liquidated in the agreement, but only at an amount reasonable in light of three things. One, the anticipated or actual harm caused by the breach. Two, the difficulty of proving loss. Three, the inconvenience or infeasibility of otherwise obtaining an adequate remedy. An unreasonably large amount is void as a penalty.

Two more points. The clause need not be conspicuous. And down-payment forfeitures are often enforced. Without a liquidated-damages term, a breaching buyer recovers its payments above the smaller of 20 percent of the price or $500, under § 2-718(2). Day 5 covers that.
Why the word or in anticipated or actual harm? It lets a clause survive if it was reasonable when made, even if the actual harm turns out different.

Problem 5-6. An oven contract with liquidated damages of $1,000 a day. The seller is 30 days late, so the clause says $30,000. The buyer's actual lost profit is $2,500. Is the clause enforceable? Likely yes. The anticipated-or-actual wording lets a clause that was reasonable when made survive. It was negotiated by merchants, based on profit discussions, the harm was hard to prove, and time was of the essence. The seller's argument: a twelvefold gap makes it a penalty.

Problem 5-9, liquidated damages versus a limitation. Liquidated damages fix the damages in advance, higher or lower than actual, and are tested for reasonableness, or penalty. A limitation eliminates or caps categories of damages; the buyer still proves its actual loss; and it is tested by failure of essential purpose and unconscionability.

segments.ask: A contract sets liquidated damages of $50,000 for a one-day delay on a $60,000 sale, with no reason to expect serious harm and easily provable losses. Enforceable?
segments.answer: No. That amount is unreasonably large in light of the anticipated or actual harm, the difficulty of proof is low, and so it is a void penalty under § 2-718(1).

segments.say: Recap. Liquidated damages are reasonable in light of anticipated or actual harm, difficulty of proof, and inconvenience of other remedies; otherwise a penalty. The or lets a clause reasonable when made survive. Limitations are tested differently, by failure of essential purpose and unconscionability.

segments.ask: State the three § 2-718(1) factors.
segments.answer: Anticipated or actual harm, difficulty of proving loss, and inconvenience or infeasibility of another adequate remedy.

segments.ask: Must a liquidated-damages clause be conspicuous?
segments.answer: No.

segments.ask: In Problem 5-6, what is the seller's best argument?
segments.answer: That the twelvefold gap between $30,000 and the $2,500 actual loss makes the clause a penalty.

episodes.title: Limited remedies and consequential exclusions: § 2-719, Problem 5-7, and Razor v. Hyundai

segments.say: Roadmap. What § 2-719 permits, exclusive versus optional remedies, failure of essential purpose, consequential-damages exclusions, and the two concentric walls of Razor.
Section 2-719(1). The parties may substitute or limit remedies: repair or replace, return and refund, caps. But an agreed remedy is optional unless expressly agreed to be exclusive.
Section 2-719(2). If an exclusive or limited remedy fails of its essential purpose, the normal UCC remedies return.

Section 2-719(3). Consequential damages may be limited or excluded unless the limitation is unconscionable. Limiting consequential damages for injury to the person in the case of consumer goods is prima facie unconscionable. Limiting them where the loss is commercial is not.

Like liquidated damages, a limitation need not be conspicuous. And personal injury isn't defined in Article 2; other law supplies it. One more point: a seller can sidestep § 2-719(3) entirely by validly disclaiming warranties, because then there's no breach.

Problem 5-7, failure of essential purpose. Three examples. A Circuit City store credit, when the retailer goes bankrupt and the credit is worthless. A repair-or-replace remedy that never fixes the defect. And replacement parts when the whole machine is destroyed.
Now Razor versus Hyundai Motor America, Illinois, 2006.

A consumer bought a new Hyundai Sonata. Hyundai's written warranty limited her remedy to repair or replacement, and separately excluded incidental and consequential damages. The car had a no-start problem that numerous repairs never fixed. The jury found the repair remedy failed of its essential purpose, and awarded $5,000 for lost value plus $3,500 for inconvenience and loss of use. The warranty and its exclusion were in the owner's manual in the glove box. She never saw them until after she signed and drove off.

Held, two parts. First, the independent approach, the majority, associated with Chatlos. The failure of the repair remedy does not automatically void the consequential-damages exclusion. The exclusion stands unless it is unconscionable under § 2-719(3). Two concentric walls. The court rejected the dependent approach of Adams versus J.I. Case, a tractor stuck in the repair shop for over a year, because that approach would make exclusions meaningless.

Second, this exclusion was unconscionable. A preprinted consumer form with no bargaining power. And, decisively, it wasn't available to her before she signed. Clear capital letters don't matter if she couldn't see it. Remanded for a new trial on § 2-714(2) damages.

Why it matters. It shows the two separate tests in § 2-719: failure of essential purpose for the limited remedy, and unconscionability for the consequential exclusion. A dissent argued the ruling burdens manufacturers and discourages written warranties.

segments.ask: A commercial buyer's contract limits remedies to repair or replace and excludes consequential damages. Repairs fail for a year, and the buyer loses $200,000 in profits. Under Razor's independent approach, can it recover the lost profits?
segments.answer: Not automatically. The failed repair remedy lets the buyer use the normal remedies, but the consequential exclusion stands unless unconscionable. Excluding commercial losses between merchants is generally not unconscionable.

segments.ask: A consumer's toaster has a consequential exclusion, and it catches fire and burns her hand. Is the exclusion enforceable as to the injury?
segments.answer: Prima facie unconscionable. Limiting consequential damages for personal injury from consumer goods is prima facie unconscionable, § 2-719(3).

segments.say: The traps. An agreed remedy is optional unless expressly exclusive. And failure of essential purpose and unconscionability are separate tests aimed at separate clauses.

Recap. Section 2-719: parties may limit remedies; exclusive only if expressly so; failure of essential purpose brings back the Code remedies; consequential exclusions stand unless unconscionable, prima facie so for consumer personal injury. Razor: the independent, two-walls approach, but this exclusion fell because she never saw it before signing.

segments.ask: What is the dependent approach, and which case represents it?
segments.answer: The view that failure of the limited remedy also voids the consequential exclusion, Adams v. J.I. Case. Razor rejected it.

segments.ask: Why was the exclusion unconscionable in Razor?
segments.answer: A preprinted consumer form with no bargaining power, and it wasn't available to her before she signed.

segments.ask: Give two examples of failure of essential purpose from Problem 5-7.
segments.answer: A store credit from a bankrupt retailer, repair that never fixes the defect, and replacement parts when the machine is destroyed.

episodes.title: The parol evidence rule: § 2-202 and the Problem 5-10 chart

segments.say: Roadmap. The rule, how it differs from the statute of frauds and the merger and NOM clauses, what it never bars, classifying the writing and the evidence, and the chart.

Section 2-202. Terms in a record the parties intended as a final expression of their agreement, as to the terms it includes, may not be contradicted by evidence of any prior agreement or of a contemporaneous oral agreement. But they may be explained or supplemented by (a), course of dealing, usage of trade, or course of performance, and (b), evidence of consistent additional terms, unless the court finds the record was also intended as a complete and exclusive statement of the terms.

Keep four things apart. The parol evidence rule is about admissibility of evidence about terms. The statute of frauds is about enforceability. A merger clause addresses prior and contemporaneous agreements. A NOM clause addresses future modifications.

The analysis. One, what extrinsic evidence is offered? Two, for what purpose? The rule applies only to evidence of an alleged term of the agreement. It does not reach evidence of a separate agreement, evidence offered for interpretation, a later modification, a formation defect like fraud, mistake, or duress, or a condition precedent.

Classify the writing. Unfinished, a tentative draft: the rule doesn't apply. Final, a partial integration, which states its terms definitively but not the whole deal: no contradiction, but consistent additional terms come in. Complete and exclusive, a full integration: no contradiction and no supplementation, except course of dealing, usage of trade, and course of performance.

Classify the evidence: explanatory, supplemental, or contradictory. Some courts require ambiguity before admitting explanatory evidence, but not for course of dealing, usage, or performance, comment 1(c). Tests for contradiction: it directly negates a term; it lacks reasonable harmony; or the parties would certainly have included it in the writing, comment 3. Versus supplementary, if it might naturally be omitted, Restatement Second § 216.
Now the Problem 5-10 chart. Two columns: final, meaning partial, and complete and exclusive.

Supplementary evidence. Oral prior, oral contemporaneous, and written prior: admissible if the writing is only final; inadmissible if complete and exclusive. Written contemporaneous: admissible if final; and if complete and exclusive, not applicable, because a contemporaneous writing is treated as part of the record. Trade practice, meaning usage of trade, course of dealing, or course of performance: admissible in both columns.

Contradictory evidence. Oral prior, oral contemporaneous, and written prior: inadmissible in both columns. Written contemporaneous: admissible against a final writing, and not applicable for complete and exclusive. And contradictory trade practice: governed by § 2-202(a) and § 1-303(e), so express terms prevail.
Two last points. A merger clause is evidence of full integration, probative but not conclusive. And getting evidence in doesn't make the fact-finder believe it.

segments.ask: A final but not complete writing for a sale of lumber says nothing about delivery. The buyer offers evidence of a prior oral agreement that the seller would deliver. Admissible?
segments.answer: Yes. A consistent additional term may supplement a final writing that is not complete and exclusive, § 2-202(b).

segments.ask: Same writing, but it says buyer will pick up. Buyer offers the same prior oral delivery agreement.
segments.answer: Inadmissible. It contradicts a term of a final writing, § 2-202.

segments.ask: The writing is complete and exclusive. The seller offers proof that the buyer fraudulently induced the deal. Barred?
segments.answer: No. The parol evidence rule never bars evidence of fraud, a formation defect.

segments.say: The trap. The rule bars prior agreements and contemporaneous oral agreements. It never bars later modifications.

Recap. Section 2-202: a final writing can't be contradicted by prior or contemporaneous oral agreements, but can be explained or supplemented by trade practice and consistent additional terms, unless it is complete and exclusive. The rule never reaches separate agreements, interpretation, later modifications, fraud, mistake, duress, or conditions precedent.

segments.ask: What evidence may supplement even a complete and exclusive writing?
segments.answer: Course of dealing, usage of trade, and course of performance.

segments.ask: State the comment 3 test for when a term would contradict rather than supplement.
segments.answer: If the parties would certainly have included it in the writing.

segments.ask: Does the parol evidence rule decide enforceability or admissibility?
segments.answer: Admissibility. The statute of frauds decides enforceability.

episodes.title: Merger clauses and the used car: Problems 5-11, 5-12, and 5-13

segments.say: Roadmap. Four clauses graded, the fiber-supplier problem, and the case where parol evidence meets § 2-316(1).
Problem 5-11 grades four clauses.
One. This represents the final agreement. Only a partial integration. Not a true merger clause.
Two. This is the complete and exclusive statement of the terms, and there are no other agreements. Best, because it tracks § 2-202(b).
Three. This supersedes all prior agreements, written or oral. Helpful, but it misses contemporaneous terms. Pair it with number two.
Four. This may not be modified except by a signed writing. That is a NOM clause. It is about future changes, not a merger clause.

Problem 5-12. A fiber supplier, and both forms say complete and exclusive. (a): a usage of trade that a supplier sells for the carpet style's market life. Admissible. Usage of trade supplements even complete records, unless carefully negated. (b): the same term from prior oral discussions. Inadmissible, because the writing is a full integration. (c)(1): usage of trade to explain the phrase support the integration of all materials. Admissible. (c)(2): prior talks to explain it. It depends; some courts require ambiguity first.
Problem 5-13, the used car. The salesperson says: never been in an accident. And: we'll fix it within 30 days. The buyer signs a writing saying AS IS, no warranty, express or implied.

The oral statements are express warranties. Section 2-316(1) would make the disclaimer inoperative as to them. But § 2-316(1) is expressly subject to § 2-202. So if the writing is final on warranties, the prior oral contradictory warranties are excluded, and the disclaimer stands. And as is kills the implied warranties.
The buyer's best routes. Fraud, which the parol evidence rule doesn't bar. Or argue the writing wasn't final, being a consumer form.

segments.ask: A buyer of a used truck signs a final writing that says as is, no express warranties. Earlier the seller said: new brakes last week. The brakes were not new. Can the buyer prove the statement as a warranty?
segments.answer: Probably not, if the writing is final on warranties. Section 2-316(1) is subject to § 2-202, so the prior oral warranty contradicting the writing is excluded. The buyer should plead fraud, which the rule doesn't bar.

segments.say: The trap. Students think § 2-316(1) always saves express warranties. It does, unless the parol evidence rule keeps the warranty out first.

Recap. The best merger clause says complete and exclusive statement, no other agreements; supersedes all prior agreements misses contemporaneous ones; a NOM clause is about the future. Usage of trade supplements even complete writings. And in Problem 5-13 the as is writing wins unless the buyer proves fraud or that the writing wasn't final.

segments.ask: Which Problem 5-11 clause best tracks § 2-202(b)?
segments.answer: This is the complete and exclusive statement of the terms; there are no other agreements.

segments.ask: Is a NOM clause a merger clause?
segments.answer: No. A NOM clause concerns future modifications. A merger clause concerns prior and contemporaneous agreements.

segments.ask: What is the buyer's best theory in Problem 5-13?
segments.answer: Fraud, which the parol evidence rule doesn't bar, or that the writing wasn't final.

episodes.title: Assignment and delegation: § 2-210 and Problems 6-1 and 6-2

segments.say: Roadmap. Rights are assigned; duties are delegated. The structure of § 2-210, the rules for each, reading prohibition clauses, § 9-406(d), and two problems.
The structure. Subsections (1) and (6), delegation. Subsections (2) and (3), assignment. Subsection (4), reading prohibition language. Subsection (5), what an assignment of the contract transfers.

Delegation, § 2-210(1). A party may perform its duty through a delegate unless otherwise agreed, or unless the other party has a substantial interest in having the original promisor perform. And delegation never relieves the delegating party of its duty or its liability for breach.
Section 2-210(6): the other party may treat any delegating assignment as creating reasonable grounds for insecurity, and may demand assurances from the assignee, under § 2-609.

Assignment, § 2-210(2). All rights are assignable except where the assignment would materially change the other party's duty, materially increase its burden or risk, or materially impair its chance of obtaining return performance. And two rights are assignable despite a contrary agreement: a right to damages for breach of the whole contract, and a right arising out of the assignor's due performance of its entire obligation.

Section 2-210(4): a clause prohibiting assignment of the contract bars only delegation, not assignment of rights. A clause saying a party may not assign its rights may only make an assignment a breach. To make an assignment ineffective, say: any attempted assignment is void.
And § 9-406(d): a term prohibiting assignment of a right to payment, an account, is ineffective. And assigning it is not a breach.

Section 2-210(5): an assignment of the contract, or of all my rights under the contract, is an assignment of rights plus a delegation of duties. The assignee's acceptance is a promise to perform, enforceable by the assignor or by the other party.
And the assignee steps into the assignor's shoes. Once notified, the obligor must pay the assignee, but it keeps its defenses.

Problem 6-1 is a grid. With no prohibition: the buyer may assign its right to the goods unless it materially changes the seller's duty, burden, risk, or chance of return performance, § 2-210(2). The seller may assign its right to payment, which rarely affects the buyer. The buyer may delegate its duty to pay, and the seller may delegate its duty to deliver, unless the other party has a substantial interest in original performance, § 2-210(1).

With a contract prohibition: the buyer's assignment of its right to the goods is not permitted, except a claim for breach of the whole, or after the buyer fully performed. The seller's assignment of its right to payment is permitted, under §§ 2-210(2) and (3) and 9-406. And delegation by either side is not permitted.

Problem 6-2, 100 steel I-beams for $20,000. (a): the seller assigns its rights to a bank. After notice, the buyer must pay the bank, keeping its defenses. (b): the contract says assignment is prohibited and void. Still effective for the right to payment, under § 9-406(d). (c): the seller assigns the contract to a manufacturer. That is an assignment plus a delegation. Standard beams mean no substantial interest in who makes them. So the buyer must accept the manufacturer's conforming goods and pay the manufacturer. The seller stays liable. And the buyer may demand assurances.

segments.ask: A contract says: neither party may assign this contract. The seller assigns its right to payment to a lender. Effective?
segments.answer: Yes. Under § 2-210(4), a ban on assigning the contract bars only delegation, and under § 9-406(d), a ban on assigning a right to payment is ineffective anyway.

segments.ask: A buyer hired a famous sculptor to carve a custom statue. The sculptor delegates the carving to an unknown apprentice. Must the buyer accept?
segments.answer: No. The buyer has a substantial interest in having the original promisor perform, § 2-210(1).

segments.say: The trap. Delegation never frees the delegator. The original party remains liable.

Recap. Delegate unless agreed otherwise or the other side has a substantial interest; the delegator stays liable; delegation is grounds for insecurity. Assign unless it materially changes duty, burden, risk, or chance of return performance. A ban on assigning the contract bars only delegation. Say void to make an assignment ineffective. And § 9-406(d) overrides bans on assigning payment rights.

segments.ask: What does an assignment of the contract transfer under § 2-210(5)?
segments.answer: Rights plus a delegation of duties, and the assignee's acceptance is a promise to perform.

segments.ask: Which two rights are assignable despite a contrary agreement?
segments.answer: A right to damages for breach of the whole contract, and a right arising from the assignor's full performance.

segments.ask: After notice of assignment, whom must the obligor pay, and what does it keep?
segments.answer: The assignee, and it keeps its defenses.

episodes.title: Termination versus cancellation: §§ 2-106 and 2-309, and Santa Fe v. Home Depot

segments.say: Roadmap. Two words that sound alike, the indefinite-term rule, and the shutter case.
Cancellation, § 2-106(4): ending the contract because of the other party's breach. The canceling party keeps its remedies for breach.
