The buyer may revoke acceptance of a lot or commercial unit whose nonconformity substantially impairs its value to him, if he accepted it (a) on the reasonable assumption that the nonconformity would be cured, and it hasn't been seasonably cured; or (b) without discovery of the nonconformity, if his acceptance was reasonably induced either by the difficulty of discovery or by the seller's assurances.

Section 2-608(2). Revocation must occur within a reasonable time after the buyer discovers or should have discovered the ground, and before any substantial change in the condition of the goods not caused by their own defects. It's not effective until the buyer notifies the seller.

Rejection versus revocation. Standard: rejection, any nonconformity; revocation, substantial impairment of value to him. Compared with § 2-612, which lacks to him; whether that changes the test is an open question. Timing: rejection, a reasonable time after tender, shorter; revocation, a reasonable time after discovery, apparently longer, comment 4. Notice content: rejection, § 2-605 can bar unstated defects; revocation, no specific content required, comment 5. Wrongful but effective? Rejection, yes. Revocation, no such thing; a revocation works only if it's both justified and properly notified, comment 5 to § 2-709. Effect: rejection is not an acceptance; revocation undoes the acceptance, and is not a cancellation, comment 1.

After a justified, effective revocation, the buyer doesn't owe the price, may cancel, and has every remedy of a buyer that rightfully rejected, § 2-711(1). It also has the same rights and duties for goods in its possession, including the § 2-711(3) lien, § 2-608(3).

Cure after revocation is unsettled. The syllogism says yes: same rights and duties as rejection, and rejection allows cure. The answer says no: § 2-608(3) speaks of duties with regard to the goods, not the seller's performance; and after a § 2-608(1)(a) revocation, cure already had its chance, though a (1)(b) revocation may be different. Lile versus Kiesel, Indiana 2007, cited only, held no right to cure after revocation.

Problem 7-26, not assigned. (A): shirt fabric discolors; 45 of 100 bolts were used. Revoke for the unused bolts. For the 45 used, the change came from the defect only if discoloration is the defect, not from the cutting and sewing. Commercial units help. (B): a motorcycle burns up. The defect caused the change, so that bar doesn't apply. Revocation mostly adds the refund; the injury is consequential. (C): a promised fuel-line repair never made. That's § 2-608(1)(a). (D): repeated leaks; the roof would have to be sawn off. Each failed repair strengthens substantial impairment, and refusing a major repair is reasonable. (E): assorted-color binders, and replacements never come. The defect was easy to see, so (1)(b) fails; (1)(a) fits.

Problem 7-27, Steelsmith and Ballistics. Was the machine accepted? Likely yes. A two-hour test, a request for a little more time, then a month's use with the problem known by June 21: § 2-606(1)(a) through (c). So rejection is too late, and revocation is the question.

Can Ballistics revoke? Probably yes. Forty instead of fifty bullets a minute is substantial impairment to a buyer needing that rate. Acceptance was induced by the difficulty of discovery: a two-hour test didn't show it, and even its engineers couldn't find the cause. Notice on July 1 is within a reasonable time after discovery, and the notice needs no particular content.

Must it accept repair? Unsettled. Section 2-508(1) is out, since the time for performance has passed. Section 2-508(2) needs reasonable grounds to think the tender acceptable. Lile says no cure after revocation; the syllogism says otherwise. If a court finds a cure right, refusing repair may be Ballistics' breach.
Use until September 1? Reasonable and necessary under the Johannsen factors: it keeps production going and mitigates. Expect an offset for the value of the use.

The result. If revocation stands: Ballistics owes no balance, recovers its $125,000 down payment, and takes cover: $750,000 minus $500,000, which is $250,000, if Epoch's machine is a reasonable substitute and not an upgrade. It holds a § 2-711(3) lien on the machine for the money it paid. If revocation fails: it owes the $375,000 balance, less § 2-714(2) damages for a machine making 40 a minute instead of 50, deducted under § 2-717.

Problem 7-28, Standard Plywood, not assigned. Usage of trade may decide whether 90 sheets per pallet conforms. Forty-five pallets instead of 50 is a shortfall, and inspection was wrongly refused. Selling for $80 and the 24-day delay raise acceptance and § 2-604 issues.

segments.ask: A buyer accepts a car, and three months later discovers a hidden transmission defect that makes it unreliable. It notifies the dealer at once. Can it revoke?
segments.answer: Yes, if the defect substantially impairs the car's value to the buyer and acceptance was reasonably induced by the difficulty of discovery, § 2-608(1)(b), with notice within a reasonable time after discovery.

segments.ask: A buyer revokes acceptance because of a small cosmetic scratch. Is the revocation effective?
segments.answer: No. Revocation requires substantial impairment, and there is no wrongful-but-effective revocation. The buyer remains bound and has only § 2-714 damages.

segments.say: Recap. Revoke for substantial impairment of value to the buyer, when acceptance rested on a reasonable assumption of cure, or was induced by difficulty of discovery or the seller's assurances. Within a reasonable time after discovery, before a substantial change not caused by the defect, with notice. No wrongful-but-effective revocation. Then the buyer has a rejecting buyer's remedies. Cure after revocation is unsettled; Lile says no.

segments.ask: Give the two grounds for revocation under § 2-608(1).
segments.answer: Acceptance on the reasonable assumption of cure that hasn't seasonably come; or acceptance without discovery, induced by difficulty of discovery or the seller's assurances.

segments.ask: What does Lile v. Kiesel hold?
segments.answer: No right to cure after revocation.

segments.ask: In Problem 7-27, what's Ballistics' cover recovery if revocation stands?
segments.answer: $250,000, the $750,000 cover minus the $500,000 contract price, plus return of its $125,000 down payment.

episodes.title: Privity and remote sellers: § 2-318, Hyundai v. Goodin, and Problems 7-31 and 7-32

segments.say: Roadmap. Vertical and horizontal privity, the three alternatives in detail, the Goodin case, who is a seller, Amazon, and two problems.

A contract claim normally needs privity. Vertical privity: a buyer in the chain of title suing a seller further up the chain, like a consumer against a manufacturer. Horizontal privity: a non-buyer outside the chain, injured by the goods. Vertical privity exists only between immediate links. A buyer who didn't buy directly from a seller is remote.

First ask whether the remote seller made any warranty to this buyer. An express warranty under § 2-313? An implied warranty under § 2-314? Or a warranty to the distributor or retailer that extends to the buyer?
Article 2 barely addresses privity. Section 2-318 offers three alternatives, and comment 3 leaves room for case law on the distributive chain.
Alternative A, the majority. Who: natural persons in the buyer's family or household, or guests in the buyer's home. Injury: in person. Vertical privity: silent, left to case law.
Alternative B. Who: any natural person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected. Injury: in person. Vertical privity: implicitly abolished.
Alternative C. Who: any person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected. Injury: injured, and some states include property or economic loss. Vertical privity: eliminated.
A seller can't exclude § 2-318's reach. But disclaimers and remedy limits that bind the buyer bind the beneficiaries too, comment 1.

Hyundai Motor America versus Goodin, Indiana 2005, a main case. Sandra Goodin bought a new Hyundai Sonata from a dealer, with a 5-year, 60,000-mile manufacturer warranty. Brake trouble began almost at once, and eight months of repairs didn't fix it. Her lawyer sought a refund. She sued Hyundai under the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act. The jury found for Hyundai on express warranty but for Goodin on the implied warranty of merchantability, and awarded $3,000. The Court of Appeals reversed for lack of privity, feeling bound by a footnote in Martin Rispens.

Held: Indiana doesn't require vertical privity between a consumer and a manufacturer for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability, even for economic loss. The footnote was dicta. Alternative A speaks only to horizontal privity and leaves vertical privity to the courts. And privity's freedom-of-contract rationale has, in the court's words, eroded to the point of invisibility for many consumer goods. Goods reach consumers through intermediaries. Warranties are marketing tools. Consumers expect merchantability. The law spreads the cost of lemons across all buyers. And a disclaimer in the dealer's buyer's order would otherwise leave her with no remedy. The privity bar began as a limit on tort claims, in Winterbottom, and was undercut by MacPherson and Henningsen.

Why it matters. The modern consumer rule, though courts remain divided. Its limits: it speaks to a consumer against a manufacturer, for goods subject to Magnuson-Moss. And damages are usually the § 2-714(2) value difference.

After Goodin. Express warranty: even privity states may not require privity. A manufacturer shouldn't escape its public claims because the buyer bought through a dealer. Open questions when privity falls away: can a remote buyer reject or revoke and get a refund from the manufacturer, and of which price? May it recover cover or market damages? Must notice go to the manufacturer, or is notice to the retailer enough? Are consequential damages tested by what the manufacturer or the retailer knew? When does the limitations period start? Which state's law applies when only one has abolished privity? Does a distributor owe the same duty?

Only sellers make implied warranties. A seller is one who sells or contracts to sell, § 2-103(1)(d), and a sale passes title, § 2-106(1). Auctioneers, brokers, and other agents without title almost always aren't sellers.

Amazon. For third-party vendors' goods, courts have held Amazon isn't a seller and makes no warranty, despite listing, payment processing, storage, and shipping. And the § 2-403(2) entrustment argument fails for three reasons: Amazon may never possess the goods, and the vendor's identity is disclosed; an entrustee isn't necessarily the seller; and Amazon's terms disclaim implied warranties anyway.

Problem 7-31. A copier. The manufacturer warrants it for 3 years from purchase and sold it June 1, 2021. The distributor disclaimed all warranties and sold it December 1, 2021. The retailer warrants it for 1 year and sold it to the buyer April 1, 2022.

(A)(1): privity is abolished; the copier fails November 1, 2022. The retailer is liable on its 1-year warranty, through April 1, 2023, and on merchantability unless disclaimed. The manufacturer is liable on its express and implied warranties if they reach the buyer; whether a warranty on order forms the buyer never saw extends to it is a real issue. The distributor isn't liable: its disclaimer works and binds those below it.

(A)(2): it fails November 1, 2023. The retailer's 1-year warranty has expired. The implied warranty requires a defect at tender, and the four years haven't run. The manufacturer's 3 years still runs on either reading of date of purchase.

(A)(3): it fails November 1, 2024. The manufacturer covers it only if purchase means the buyer's purchase, running to April 1, 2025, not the distributor's, which ended June 1, 2024. Implied warranties remain only if the defect existed at tender and suit is timely under § 2-725.

(B): privity not abolished. The implied claim runs only against the retailer. An express claim against the manufacturer may survive, though this warranty wasn't a public statement. And the retailer has no recourse past the distributor's disclaimer: the gap privity creates.

(C): a fire destroys the vice president's home, with no one injured. The VP isn't the buyer, so this is horizontal. Alternative A: no. The VP isn't family, household, or a guest of a corporate buyer, and wasn't injured in person. Alternative B: no; it's property loss only. Alternative C: yes, where injured includes property, against the retailer, and the manufacturer, since vertical privity is gone. The distributor is still protected by its disclaimer. And tort remains.

Problem 7-32. A homeowner and a renovator, in a privity state. Make the homeowner a party in privity with the appliance seller: have the homeowner buy directly, or have the renovator buy as the homeowner's agent. Or have the renovator assign its warranty rights to the homeowner under § 2-210, and get the seller to name the homeowner an intended beneficiary. The renovation contract alone can't bind the seller. And add the renovator's own express warranty.

segments.ask: In an Alternative A state, a buyer's houseguest is burned when a defective space heater explodes. Can the guest sue the retailer for breach of warranty?
segments.answer: Yes. A guest in the buyer's home, injured in person, is covered by Alternative A.

segments.ask: In the same state, a neighbor's house burns because of the same heater, but no one is hurt. Can the neighbor sue in warranty?
segments.answer: No under Alternative A. The neighbor isn't family, household, or a guest, and wasn't injured in person. Tort remains.

segments.say: Recap. Vertical privity runs up the chain; horizontal reaches non-buyers. Alternative A: family, household, guests, personal injury. B: any natural person reasonably expected, personal injury. C: any person, and some states include property. Goodin: no vertical privity for a consumer's merchantability claim against a manufacturer. Only sellers warrant, and Amazon generally isn't one for third-party goods.

segments.ask: In Goodin, what did the jury find, and what did the Indiana Supreme Court hold?
segments.answer: For Hyundai on express warranty, for Goodin on implied merchantability, $3,000. The court held no vertical privity is required for a consumer's implied-warranty claim against a manufacturer, even for economic loss.

segments.ask: Does a disclaimer binding the buyer bind a § 2-318 beneficiary?
segments.answer: Yes, comment 1. But the seller can't exclude § 2-318's reach.

segments.ask: Name the three reasons the entrustment argument against Amazon fails.
segments.answer: Amazon may never possess the goods and the vendor is disclosed; an entrustee isn't necessarily the seller; and Amazon's terms disclaim implied warranties.

episodes.title: Day 4 closing quiz

segments.say: Cumulative quiz, Days 1 to 4.

segments.ask: Name the three ways a buyer can get the goods themselves.
segments.answer: Specific performance and replevin under § 2-716, and recovery of identified prepaid goods under § 2-502.

segments.ask: A buyer covers at a lower price than the contract. Can it use market damages instead?
segments.answer: No. Having covered, it can't switch to § 2-713, unless the purchase wasn't a true substitute.

segments.ask: Market damages under § 2-713 are measured when and where?
segments.answer: When the buyer learned of the breach, at the place for tender, or the place of arrival after rejection on arrival or revocation.

segments.ask: In an installment contract, when can a buyer cancel the whole?
segments.answer: When a nonconformity in one or more installments substantially impairs the value of the whole contract, § 2-612(3).

segments.ask: A buyer with a right to reject gives late notice. Result?
segments.answer: Ineffective rejection, so acceptance. It owes the price but has § 2-714 damages with timely § 2-607(3)(a) notice.

segments.ask: What two kinds of cure does § 2-508 allow?
segments.answer: Within the contract time on seasonable notice; or a further reasonable time if the seller reasonably believed the tender would be acceptable.

segments.ask: State the § 2-714(2) formula.
segments.answer: Value as warranted minus value as accepted, at the time and place of acceptance, unless special circumstances show different proximate damages.

segments.ask: Is there such a thing as a wrongful but effective revocation?
segments.answer: No. Revocation must be justified and properly notified.

segments.ask: Under Alternative B, who is protected?
segments.answer: Any natural person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected, who is injured in person.

segments.ask: From Day 3: what makes a consequential-damages exclusion for consumer personal injury suspect?
segments.answer: It is prima facie unconscionable, § 2-719(3).

segments.ask: From Day 2: who gives the warranty of non-infringement?
segments.answer: A merchant regularly dealing in goods of the kind, unless the buyer furnished specifications.

segments.ask: From Day 1: in Casazza, did promissory estoppel save the buyer?
segments.answer: No. His reliance wasn't the kind that makes refusal a fraud.

segments.say: That's Day 4. Tomorrow, the last day: the seller's remedies, leases, and the full review.
